summary: Describes a TFTP option that lets client and server negotiate a block size better suited to the network medium. It was replaced by RFC 2348.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1783 lets TFTP clients and servers agree to transfer data in blocks larger than the protocol's 512-byte default. Larger blocks can reduce the number of packets, but blocks bigger than the path MTU can cause fragmentation.

questions: how does tftp negotiate block size
what is the tftp blksize range
subtitle: A TFTP option for agreeing on a data block size that fits the network.

tldr.problem: TFTP's 512-byte default blocks can be inefficient on a local network that can carry larger packets.
tldr.mechanism: The client includes a blksize option in its read or write request. The server can answer with an Option Acknowledgment that chooses a size no larger than the proposal.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1783 updates RFC 1350 and was later obsoleted by RFC 2348.

sections.title: Why TFTP Can Use Larger Blocks
sections.content:
TFTP is a simple, lock-step file transfer protocol used to get or put files on a remote host. One use described by the RFC is booting diskless nodes on a local area network. Its default block size is 512 bytes, which is not efficient when the network MTU is 1500 bytes or greater.

RFC 1783 defines an option so the client and server can negotiate a block size better suited to the network medium.
sections.plainLanguage: TFTP sends a file in blocks and waits for acknowledgments. On networks that can carry larger packets, bigger blocks can mean fewer exchanges.

sections.title: Requesting and Agreeing on a Block Size
sections.content:
The client adds the case-insensitive option name blksize and a proposed number of octets to its Read Request or Write Request. The number is an ASCII string from 8 through 65464, inclusive, terminated by a null character. The RFC gives 1432 bytes as an example sized to fit an Ethernet MTU after UDP and IP headers.

If willing to accept the option, the server sends an Option Acknowledgment with a value no greater than the client's proposal. The client must use that value or send an ERROR packet with code 8 to end the transfer. The usual final-block rule remains: a data packet shorter than the negotiated block size ends the transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: The client proposes a block size in its first request. The server can agree to that size or a smaller one, and the client must use the agreed value.

sections.title: Transfer Speed and Path Limits
sections.content:
In the RFC's tests on a lightly loaded Ethernet, the measured transfer time fell as block size increased. For example, the reported time without an intermediate gateway was 23.85 seconds at 512 bytes and 6.85 seconds at 4096 bytes for the test file.

Fewer data blocks also mean fewer acknowledgments and less per-packet processing. However, when a block exceeds the path MTU, IP fragmentation and reassembly add overhead; the RFC notes that this is more noticeable when the path has more gateways. The memo does not discuss security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC's Ethernet tests found that larger blocks reduced transfer time by reducing packets and acknowledgments. A block that is too large for the route can instead add fragmentation work.

references.text: Sollins, K., "The TFTP Protocol (Revision 2)", STD 33, RFC 1350, July 1992.
Malkin, G. and A. Harkin, "TFTP Option Extension", RFC 1782, March 1995.
